findings.headline: Council approved £17m of new prudential borrowing across 2026/27–2028/29 to fund regeneration and leisure schemes.
findings.detail: In addition to existing debt, the council approved new prudential borrowing of £17.0m spread across 2026/27 to 2028/29 to fund the Pride in Place programme, Local Regeneration Fund, Leisure schemes, and Playing Pitch Investment. This represents new debt commitments that will create future revenue consequences through interest and eventual repayment, alongside the £27m in capital receipts expected from NuPlace Ltd.
findings.matters: New borrowing commitments increase the council's debt burden and future interest costs at a time when the council is already under demand pressure in core services. The council needs to demonstrate it can service this debt and maintain its financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £17.0m new prudential borrowing 2026/27–2028/29; £27m additional capital receipts expected from NuPlace
findings.quote: additional prudential borrowing of £17.0m across 2026/27 to 2028/29 to support the Pride in Place programme, Local Regeneration Fund, Leisure schemes and Playing Pitch Investment.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection fell 0.41% below target to 96.89%, driven by Universal Credit transitions reducing support.
findings.detail: Council Tax collection declined to 96.89% against a 97.3% target, and fell 0.2 percentage points year-on-year (prior year 97.1%). The council identified the primary cause as benefit recipients transitioning from legacy benefits to Universal Credit and receiving less Council Tax Reduction as a result. While the council continues to pursue all debt vigorously, this represents a structural headwind to collection rates.
findings.matters: This is a structural change in the council's tax base that will not reverse. As more claimants transition to Universal Credit, the council should expect lower collection rates as a permanent feature, reducing the income available for services.
findings.figures: 96.89% actual vs 97.3% target (0.41% shortfall); 0.2 percentage point decline vs prior year
findings.quote: A major reason for this fall in performance is the number of benefit recipients that have transitioned from legacy benefits to Universal Credit and are receiving less Council Tax Reduction as a result.

findings.headline: Sales Ledger debt collection shortfall of 3.34%, driven by a large unpaid balance from the Integrated Care Board.
findings.detail: Sales Ledger outstanding debt stood at 9.34% against a target of 6%, a shortfall of £3.77m on a £106.6m debt base. The council identified a large balance owing from the Integrated Care Board (ICB) which it is actively pursuing. This includes both general debt and Social Care debt from council service provision. The council notes ledger can fluctuate month to month but this year-end figure is outside target.
findings.matters: Income collection shortfalls reduce resources available for services. A large single debtor (the ICB) represents concentration risk — if that debt proves uncollectable, it creates a sudden pressure. Social Care debt from the health system is particularly concerning given ASC budget pressures.
findings.figures: £9.771m outstanding debt (9.34% of £106.6m annual); £3.34% shortfall from 6% target
findings.quote: Sales ledger is outside of target although can tend to fluctuate from one month to the next. There is a large balance outstanding with the ICB which we are seeking to recover.

findings.headline: Children's Safeguarding overspent by £2.8m from placement volume and cost inflation.
findings.detail: Children in Care placements overspent by £4.38m driven by both increases in the number of children in care and inflation in placement costs. The service made savings from early intervention and review work, but could not offset the volume and cost growth. This is despite Health funding and grant income offsetting some costs. The overspend signals demand is outpacing mitigation efforts.
findings.matters: This is a statutory duty area and overspends here cannot be reduced by cutting service — the council must meet its safeguarding obligations. The volume and cost growth suggests these pressures will persist, putting future budgets under strain.
findings.figures: £2.8m total overspend in Children's Safeguarding; £4.38m overspend on CIC placements before offsetting items
findings.quote: Children in Care, Leaving Care Team & Speciality Services, Family Solutions: CIC Placement, Post 16 Staying Put & Leaving Care Support – increases in placement numbers and inflation associated with the cost of placements outweighed savings from the work with Impower and ongoing work on prevention, early intervention and review of all placement costs

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit of £9.21m becomes a council liability from 2028 when the statutory override ends.
findings.detail: The DSG overspent by £4.55m in 2025/26, combined with a carried-forward deficit of £4.66m from prior year, creating a total deficit of £9.21m. The government's statutory override protecting councils from this liability ends 31 March 2028, after which Telford & Wrekin must fund 10% of the deficit up to 2025/26 (£0.92m) plus a share of deficits accruing in 2026/27 and 2027/28. This is a national issue (£3.5bn net deficit) but is now a future financial commitment.
findings.matters: This represents a multi-million pound unfunded liability that materialises in 2-3 years. The council will need to find resources or make savings to cover it at a time when its other pressures (ASC, Children's) are still growing. It also shows education funding is structurally broken at the national level.
findings.figures: £9.21m DSG deficit carried to 2026/27; £0.92m becomes council's liability from 2028; £4.55m overspend in 2025/26 alone; national net DSG deficit £3.5bn
findings.quote: Excluding funds passed to academies and colleges, Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) totalled £135.729m in 2025/26. There was an overspend of £4.55m during the year. As a deficit balance of £4.66m had been carried forward into 2025/26 from the previous year, a year-end deficit of £9.21m has been carried forward to 2026/27.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care required £6.8m additional investment within the year despite £7.9m already budgeted.
findings.detail: The council needed to deploy additional contingency funds of £6.8m in Adult Social Care during 2025/26, following the £7.9m of additional investment already included in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy. The pressures were driven by market price increases, more complex needs, higher demand, and longer periods of care being required. This demonstrates ASC costs are outpacing even the council's expanded budget provision.
findings.matters: Adult Social Care is the largest single budget line (£81.9m net revenue budget) and the additional requirement suggests structural cost growth that budgets may not be capturing. This is material to forecasting the council's future financial sustainability.
findings.figures: £6.8m additional investment in 2025/26 on top of £7.9m already in MTFS; total ASC outturn £88.7m vs budget £82.0m
findings.quote: The prudent inclusion of specific contingencies within the budget have helped to support the key pressure area of Adult Social Care (ASC), with £6.8m essential additional investment being required relating to the cost of providing care and support across all client groups. This includes the impact of market price increases, more complex needs, higher demand and longer periods of care being required.

findings.headline: Treasury operations recorded a £0.27m net pressure in 2025/26 due to elevated borrowing rates exceeding investment returns
findings.detail: The council's treasury strategy aims to balance security, liquidity and yield. In 2025/26, however, the gap between borrowing costs and investment returns widened, creating a net pressure of £0.27m against budget. Financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream increased from 6.7% (original budget) to 6.9% (outturn), driven by elevated interest rates on borrowing compared to returns on short-term investments.
findings.matters: If rates remain elevated while investment returns stay suppressed, this margin pressure will persist into 2026/27, further squeezing financial headroom and increasing effective debt service costs.
findings.figures: Net treasury pressure £0.27m in 2025/26. Financing costs as proportion of net revenue stream: original 6.7%, outturn 6.9%. Treasury investments held under 1 year: £23.866m (2025/26 outturn).
findings.quote: Overall, a net pressure of £0.27m was realised against budget for the year. The pressure arose from elevated interest rates associated with borrowing compared to interest rates for investments

findings.headline: External debt projected to rise from £492.7m to £576.1m (17% increase); authorised borrowing limit raised from £665m to £840m
findings.detail: Following the capital programme increase, gross external debt is projected to grow by £83.4m (16.9%) between 2025/26 outturn and 2026/27 projection. The loans Capital Financing Requirement rises from £629.2m to £707.0m. To accommodate this growth, the council has increased its Authorised Limit for borrowing from £665m to £840m and its Operational Boundary from £645m to £820m—an increase of £175m in headroom.
findings.matters: A 17% year-on-year increase in external debt is material and signals either accelerating capital investment or schemes coming online. Lenders assess leverage and debt service burden; this trajectory warrants understanding whether it is sustainable over the medium term.
findings.figures: External debt 2025/26 outturn £492.660m; 2026/27 projection £576.065m (difference £83.405m). Loans CFR: £629.211m (2025/26) to £707.005m (2026/27, difference £77.794m). Authorised Limit increasing from £665m to £840m.
findings.quote: Gross borrowing (External Debt) 502.877 [2025/26 original] 492.660 [2025/26 outturn] ... 565.727 [2026/27 original] 576.065 [2026/27 projection]

findings.headline: Capital expenditure for 2026/27 projected at £164.9m—42% above original budget of £116.3m—subject to rephasing review in September
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital budget was originally set at £116.316m. As of 31 May 2026, projections show £164.860m—a jump of £48.5m or 42%. The document flags this as uncertain: 'subject to rephasing to be reported as part of the 2026/27 Financial Monitoring report to Cabinet in September 2026'. This increase is also inconsistent with 2025/26 delivery, where capital spend came in £38.3m below budget (£113.3m actual vs £151.6m planned).
findings.matters: If delivered as projected, this requires an additional £48.5m in borrowing beyond the original plan. Combined with the 2025/26 underspend, it suggests material volatility in the capital programme—either delivery risk or unconfirmed scope increases. Lenders would want clarity on whether this is real or speculative.
findings.figures: 2026/27 original budget £116.316m; projection at 31 May 2026 £164.860m (+£48.544m or +42%). For comparison, 2025/26 budget was £151.563m but outturn was £113.253m (underspend £38.31m).
findings.quote: subject to rephasing to be reported as part of the 2026/27 Financial Monitoring report to Cabinet in September 2026

findings.headline: Interest rate forecast has deteriorated materially due to Middle East conflict and elevated inflation; cuts now postponed to mid-2027
findings.detail: The council's original forecast expected significant rate reductions across 2025/26. Instead, the Bank of England base rate fell only to 3.75% by March 2026. The council explicitly attributes this to inflation concerns and the Iran/Middle East conflict starting 28 February 2026, which created market instability. The forecast now expects rates held at 3.75% until mid-2027, then declining to 3.25% by March 2028—much later than originally planned. This delays refinancing relief and extends the period of elevated borrowing costs.
findings.matters: Borrowing costs will remain elevated throughout 2026/27 and into 2027, materially increasing the council's debt service costs above what was budgeted in the Medium-Term Financial Strategy.
findings.figures: Bank of England base rate 4.5% (April 2025) falling to 3.75% (March 2026), expected to remain at 3.75% through to mid-2027. Original forecast expected significant reductions; actual outturn showed only 0.75% cut over the year.
findings.quote: the war in Iran and across large parts of the Middle East, which commenced on 28 February 2026, has led to a period of instability within the markets and interest rates have remained elevated with any cuts in the short-term deemed unlikely

findings.headline: Emergency response capability is acknowledged to be constrained by human resources for any prolonged incident despite established business continuity plans
findings.detail: The Council Emergency Plan was tested and updated in 2025 with business continuity plans and emergency coordination in place. However, the risk register explicitly acknowledges a known gap: 'However prolonged incidents will result in a significant human resource challenge', indicating the council recognises it cannot fully execute a sustained emergency response.
findings.matters: Resilience to prolonged shocks (pandemic-scale, major weather event) requires adequate human resource capacity to deploy; acknowledged constraints indicate business continuity risk that could disrupt service delivery
findings.figures: No figures; resource constraint acknowledged but unquantified
findings.quote: However prolonged incidents will result in a significant human resource challenge

findings.headline: Project delivery is flagged as Very High risk and remains Medium risk even with new oversight; Levelling Up Fund and Towns Fund schemes specifically monitored
findings.detail: The risk register identifies that increasing numbers of projects combined with resource constraints create project failure risk. A Major Projects Board has been established with monthly monitoring for schemes funded by Levelling Up Fund and Towns Fund. Despite these controls, the risk remains Medium likelihood, indicating project delivery has been genuinely challenging.
findings.matters: If capital projects (particularly government-funded regeneration with tight conditions and time deadlines) aren't being delivered on schedule or to budget, it affects growth strategy implementation and may impact expected revenues or economic benefits
findings.figures: Risk reduced from Very High to Medium with controls, specific projects not detailed
findings.quote: Increasing number of projects and resource challenges to deliver those projects leads to project failure and inability to continue to deliver existing council services effectively and efficiently

findings.headline: Significant uncommitted reserves of £21.7m are being relied upon to support medium-term financial strategy, alongside £3.95m annual contingency
findings.detail: The council explicitly depends on £21.7m of uncommitted balances held within the Budget Strategy Reserve to manage financial pressures from austerity, demand growth, inflation, and COVID impacts. An additional £3.95m general contingency is held annually, with £3.5m specifically allocated for contract inflation and pay awards.
findings.matters: Reserve level indicates the financial buffer available to absorb unexpected pressures; for a lender assessing financial resilience, the adequacy and depletion trend of reserves is critical
findings.figures: £21.7m uncommitted balances, £3.95m budget contingency, £3.5m allocated for inflation/pay awards
findings.quote: significant level (£21.7m) of uncommitted balances available, held within the Budget Strategy Reserve to support the Council's Medium Term Financial Strategy

findings.headline: Adult Social Care and Children's Safeguarding, representing two-thirds of council budget, received substantial increases but require formal cost improvement plans to manage demand pressure
findings.detail: The council increased Adult Social Care investment by £15.8m (to £97m total) and Children's Safeguarding by £2.7m (to £52m total). Combined budget of ~£150m represents two-thirds of net budget. Despite these increases, formal Cost Improvement Plans are in place for both services and monitored by senior officers and members, indicating ongoing demand pressures. Additional £3.5m provided for contract inflation and pay awards in 2026/27.
findings.matters: Social care is typically the largest and fastest-growing pressure in councils; a lender must assess whether the council can sustainably fund demographic and cost trends while maintaining other services
findings.figures: £15.8m increase to Adult Social Care (total £97m), £2.7m increase to Children's Safeguarding (total £52m), combined £150m (two-thirds of net budget), £3.5m for inflation and pay awards, both services require active Cost Improvement Plans
findings.quote: The Council increased investment into Adult Social Care services by £15.8m in 2026/27. The Council's net budget for Adult Social Care is over £97m in 2026/27... The Council has increased investment into Children's Safeguarding by £2.7m in 2026/27 with the net budget totalling £52m in 2026/27... The combined total net budget allocation for these services is nearly of £150m

findings.paper_title: TWC Value for Money risk assessment
findings.headline: Medium-term savings plan of £19.1m requires £5.6m from income generation via Nuplace and trading, creating dependency on commercial returns.
findings.detail: The MTFS requires £19.1m in savings for 2026/27 onwards: £12m from service redesign and £5.6m from income generated by Nuplace (the council's housing company) and other trading operations. These commercial returns are needed to bridge the gap left by service redesign, meaning the budget plan carries execution risk on both fronts.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that this plan is realistic and that the council is not betting the budget on commercial returns that might not materialise; the £5.6m income element is discretionary income from council-owned enterprises, not statutory funding.
findings.figures: £19.1m total savings: £12.0m service redesign, £5.6m from Nuplace and trading income
findings.quote: For 2026/27 and onwards to 2028/29, the updated MTFS outlines proposed budgeted savings of £19.1m, including £12.0m attributed to service review / redesign and £5.6m from income generation from Nuplace and other trading operations.

findings.paper_title: TWC Value for Money risk assessment
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs deficit nearly doubled in a single year to £9.21m, driven by SEND demand.
findings.detail: The DSG High Needs deficit increased from £4.66m (March 2025) to £9.21m (March 2026) due to increasing demand and costs for SEND provision. The council is relying on the statutory override (in place until March 2028) and expected government funding to support 90% of historic deficits to manage this pressure.
findings.matters: A doubling deficit in one year on a statutory account signals rapid underlying cost growth outside normal budget control; though mitigated by override and government support, it represents material uncertainty in the medium-term position.
findings.figures: DSG High Needs deficit £4.66m (2025) to £9.21m (2026); government expected to fund 90% of historic deficits
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) High Needs Block remains a significant financial pressure, with the deficit increasing from £4.66m at 31 March 2025 to £9.21m at 31 March 2026 as a result of increasing demand and costs associated with SEND provision.

findings.paper_title: TWC Value for Money risk assessment
findings.headline: Adult Social Care, Children's Safeguarding and Education overran budget by £11.2m combined; 2025/26 was balanced only by releasing contingencies and unbudgeted reserves.
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspent by £6.8m, Children's Safeguarding and Family Support by £2.8m, and Education and Skills by £1.6m. The council reported a £0.133m underspend against a £167.6m net budget only because these overspends were offset by releasing budgeted contingencies and Council-wide unbudgeted reserves. This suggests structural cost pressures rather than one-off variances.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council can balance its budget from operations or whether it is relying on drawing down contingencies to mask real service cost pressures in the highest-cost, highest-demand areas.
findings.figures: £6.8m Adult Social Care overspend, £2.8m Children's Safeguarding overspend, £1.6m Education and Skills overspend; overall £0.133m underspend on £167.6m revenue budget
findings.quote: This was achieved despite significant service pressures, including a £6.8m overspend in Adult Social Care, a £2.8m overspend in Children's Safeguarding and Family Support and a £1.6m overspend in Education and Skills. This was offset by the release of budgeted contingencies and other Council wide unbudgeted reserves.

findings.headline: Council faces ongoing staffing challenges with reduction in appropriately skilled staff in some service areas
findings.detail: The AGS action plan identifies reduction in appropriately skilled staff in some service areas due to recruitment challenges in local government, particularly for certain professions. This results in some single points of failure or reliance on temporary staffing. Ongoing work on workforce strategy, apprenticeships and recruitment channels continues.
findings.matters: Single points of failure increase operational and financial control risks; temporary staffing reduces service consistency and may increase costs; affects council's resilience and execution capability
findings.figures: Specific services and numbers not quantified; characterised as 'some service areas' and 'some single points of failure'
findings.quote: Recruitment of staff in local government, particularly in some professions, continues to be challenging. This results in some single points of failure or the use of temporary staff, although the work undertaken on the Workforce Strategy presents opportunity to address this challenge.

findings.headline: Children's Services achieved £9.6m cost avoidance through placement cost reductions via IMPOWER Valuing Care partnership
findings.detail: Children's Services partnership with IMPOWER on 'Valuing Care' approach achieved £9.6m in cost savings related to changes in placement costs in 2025/26. A cost improvement plan continues to be monitored by Senior Management Team and members, with other savings streams being explored.
findings.matters: Shows the council can deliver material savings (£9.6m) in high-cost service areas through structured programmes; placement costs are major budget items for children's services
findings.figures: £9.6m cost avoidance from placement cost changes
findings.quote: This work also looks at cost savings / avoidance including saving of £9.6 m related to changes in placement costs. Other savings streams are also being explored.

findings.headline: Council has delivered £195.3m in cumulative savings since 2009 but requires £16.7m additional savings by end of 2026/27
findings.detail: The council reports cumulative ongoing savings and additional income of £195.3m delivered by end of 2025/26. A further £16.7m in savings/additional income is targeted for delivery by end of 2026/27. This reflects sustained financial pressure primarily driven by increased Adult Social Care demand.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council has executed substantial difficult savings over 15+ years but faces continued budget constraint; a lender needs assurance of ongoing delivery capability
findings.figures: £195.3m cumulative savings (2009-2026), £16.7m additional target for 2026/27
findings.quote: £195.3m of ongoing savings/additional income will have been delivered by the end of 2025/26 with a further £16.7m ongoing savings/additional income to be delivered by the end of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Joint Report on the Internal Audit Annual Report 202526 The Audit Committee Report The 202627
findings.headline: Staffing and supervisory capacity reductions are explicitly flagged as threatening the effectiveness of financial controls.
findings.detail: The council's financial implications section identifies reductions in staffing levels and supervisory capacity across the organisation as a risk factor that 'may impact the effectiveness of financial controls and increase the risk of errors or non-compliance'. This is highlighted alongside continued budget pressure as a material challenge for 2026/27. The Internal Audit Team itself operates at 3.4 full-time equivalents.
findings.matters: Reduced supervisory capacity directly reduces the ability to detect and prevent financial control failures; this is a material control risk for any lender.
findings.figures: Internal Audit Team: 3.4 full-time equivalents
findings.quote: The report highlights continued pressure on the Council's budget strategy, alongside reductions in staffing levels and supervisory capacity, which may impact the effectiveness of financial controls and increase the risk of errors or non-compliance.

findings.paper_title: Joint Report on the Internal Audit Annual Report 202526 The Audit Committee Report The 202627
findings.headline: Financial Regulation recommendations have trebled from 14% to 28% of audit findings with no identified cause.
findings.detail: In 2025/26, Financial Regulation recommendations increased to 28% of all audit recommendations, up from 16% in 2024/25 and 14% in 2023/24. The Internal Audit team provides no explanation for this sharp rise, stating only that there was 'no thematic reason for this increase'. The paper notes that as part of good governance, Internal Audit will continue to remind services of requirements to comply with these regulations.
findings.matters: A consistent rise in financial regulation breaches across service areas may indicate weakening compliance culture or control discipline, which would concern any lender assessing the council's financial governance.
findings.quote: In 2025/26 the % of Financial Regulation recommendations increased to 28% from 16% in 2024/25 and 14% in 2023/24. There was no thematic reason for this increase.

findings.headline: Council plans £74.6m prudential borrowing in 2026/27 including material commercial investments in NuPlace and property portfolio
findings.detail: Prudential indicators show planned borrowing of £74.6m in 2026/27, £59.6m in 2027/28, and £22.4m in 2028/29. The council notes these figures include further investment in NuPlace (the council's wholly owned housing company) and a property investment portfolio, both expected to generate returns exceeding associated debt charges. Prudential borrowing represents 64% of total capital financing in 2026/27. The capital financing requirement grows from £676.1m to £811.5m over three years.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council's borrowing is sustainable and whether its financial position is dependent on commercial investments generating expected returns. If investments underperform, this could impact the council's ability to service debt.
findings.quote: These figures include further investment in NuPlace, the Council's wholly owned Housing Company, and Property Investment Portfolio both of which should generate returns for the Council well in excess of the associated debt charges

findings.headline: 15 neighbourhoods fall in the 10% most deprived nationally, despite overall council prosperity
findings.detail: Telford & Wrekin has attracted £70m MoD investment and £80m+ from Magna and presents as a growth hub, yet 15 neighbourhoods rank in the 10% most deprived nationally. This concentration of deprivation can create volatile demand for social care and children's services.
findings.matters: Concentrated deprivation in specific areas drives higher spending on social support, children's services, and welfare, making per-capita budget assumptions unreliable and creating risk of localized spending pressures.
findings.figures: 15 neighbourhoods in 10% most deprived nationally
findings.quote: Although at face value it is a successful and attractive place to live, Telford & Wrekin is an area of contrast with 15 neighbourhoods ranked in the 10% most deprived nationally

findings.headline: Council funding increasingly reliant on commercial ventures and external grants rather than core government funding
findings.detail: The strategy emphasises income from solar farms (£0.8m/year), a housing company (Nuplace, 600 homes built aiming for 900+), a growth fund (£10.3m projected 2025/26), property portfolio (£10m+/year), plus external grants including £20m Levelling Up, £22.3m Town's Fund, and others. The council notes it receives only 49% of new business rates generated.
findings.matters: Commercial income is volatile and exposed to economic downturns (property values, solar farm performance); grants can be withdrawn or reduced. This creates revenue instability and reduces predictability of funding.
findings.figures: Solar farm £0.8m/year (£5.2m cumulative to March 2025); Growth Fund £10.3m projected 2025/26; property portfolio over £10m/year; external funding: £20m Levelling Up, £22.3m Town's Fund, £18.79m Marches LEP, £9.8m regeneration, £1.37m decarbonisation
findings.quote: Net additional income from the Telford Growth Fund is projected to exceed £10.3m in 2025/26" and "property investment portfolio – a property investment portfolio delivering over £10m income per annum from rental income.

findings.headline: Population growth of 14.9% in a decade, nearly double the England average, concentrated in elderly cohort growing 27.6%
findings.detail: Telford & Wrekin's population grew from ~170,000 to 195,952 between 2014-2024, projected to exceed 200,000 within 2-3 years. People aged 65+ increased by 27.6% (7,568 people), compared to 15.5% for England. 49% of this growth is from internal migration, suggesting continuing upward pressure.
findings.matters: Rapid aging in a growing population drives sustained demand for Adult Social Care, the largest budget pressure on councils, while government funding settlement does not track demographic change. This creates an ongoing structural deficit.
findings.figures: Population growth 14.9% vs 7.8% for England; 65+ cohort growth 27.6% vs 15.5% for England; population projected to exceed 200,000 in 2-3 years
findings.quote: Between 2014 and 2024 the borough's population grew by 14.9%. This was the greatest upper tier local authority increase in the West Midlands Region and almost double that of England (7.8%). People aged 65 and over are the fastest growing age group in the borough, increasing by 27.6% (7,568 people) between 2014 and 2024.

findings.headline: Council warns that future savings will be 'significantly more challenging' as easy efficiency gains are exhausted
findings.detail: After delivering £195.3m in cumulative savings over 17 years, the council now plans only £15.7m in new savings for 2026/27, then £0.7m and £0.8m in subsequent years. The strategy explicitly states it must manage ongoing deficits through efficiency that is becoming harder to find, requiring 'medium term planning and increased certainty over grant levels'.
findings.matters: This signals the council has harvested easy wins and faces a structural budget challenge. Future years' savings targets may not be achievable without service cuts or tax rises, making budget forecasts less reliable.
findings.quote: Future savings will be significantly more challenging as the "low hanging fruit" has already been harvested making medium term planning and increased certainty over grant levels essential.

findings.headline: Limited land holdings as former new town constrains ability to reduce borrowing through asset sales
findings.detail: Council explicitly acknowledges constrained capacity to generate capital receipts through disposals compared to other authorities. This structural constraint means 52.8% of the capital programme (£230.2m) must be funded by prudential borrowing, peaking at £74.6m in 2026/27, with limited flexibility to reduce debt if circumstances change.
findings.matters: Structural constraint on asset sales locks council into revenue-funded debt servicing with limited flexibility if revenues fall or interest rates rise
findings.figures: £230.2m prudential borrowing (52.8% of total); peak year 2026/27: £74.6m; capital receipts only £17.8m (4% of programme)
findings.quote: As a former new town area, with the Council having limited land and asset holdings, we have a more limited capacity to generate capital receipts through disposals than some other authorities.

findings.headline: Maintenance backlog on operational property has grown 60% in five years to £9m
findings.detail: Asset management data shows operational property condition backlog grew from £5.6m (2020) to £9.0m (2025), while schools backlog stands at £15.4m. The 2026/27 investment of only £1.2m on £9.0m operational backlog means the gap is widening. Growing maintenance backlogs typically precede emergency repairs and service disruption.
findings.matters: Deferred maintenance becomes more expensive to fix; growing backlog signals budget constraints preventing preventative spending and indicates future cost pressures
findings.figures: Operational backlog 2020: £5.6m to 2025: £9.0m (60% increase); Schools: £15.4m; 2026/27 investment: £1.2m operational, £1.6m schools
findings.quote: The Council's Asset Management Plan has identified a condition backlog of £9.0m for Operational Properties (excluding schools) and £15.4m for Schools / Education properties.

findings.headline: Budget contingency reserve of £21.7m is static across the five-year forecast, showing no flexibility for new pressures.
findings.detail: The council's largest single reserve is a Budget Strategy Reserve for budget contingency of £21.7m. This balance remains unchanged throughout the entire forecast period (2025/26 through 2029/30), indicating it is fully committed to support the Medium Term Financial Strategy and provides no financial headroom.
findings.matters: A static contingency reserve suggests limited capacity to absorb unexpected spending pressures or income shortfalls; the council may be running without a safety margin.
findings.figures: £21.7m (static throughout forecast period)
findings.quote: To support Medium Term Financial Strategy

findings.headline: Hadley PFI sinking fund of £1.5m is locked into systematic drawdowns through 2030, representing fixed future obligations.
findings.detail: The council holds a Hadley PFI Sinking Fund of £1.5m at April 2025, which is declining by £272k in the first year and £329k in the second year, continuing through the forecast. This represents pre-committed PFI financing obligations that will consume reserves predictably over the five-year period.
findings.matters: PFI obligations are contractually fixed and inflexible; this long-term drain on reserves is already committed and cannot be reduced if budget pressures emerge elsewhere.
findings.figures: Hadley PFI Sinking Fund £1.5m declining to £464k by 2029/30 with annual drawdowns of £272k, £329k, £375k, and £64k
findings.quote: PFI equalisation account; based on funding model

findings.headline: Transport bus subsidy reserve of £491k is being drawn down to fund routes following new Arriva contract commencing August 2025.
findings.detail: The council holds a £491k Transport Bus Subsidy reserve that is declining over the forecast period. The notes indicate this is funding subsidised bus routes and is supporting a new commercial contract with Arriva starting August 2025. The balance falls from £491k to £368k in year one.
findings.matters: Ongoing bus subsidy from reserves indicates the council is using reserves to fund a discretionary service; if the subsidy is inadequate or the Arriva contract becomes unviable, additional pressure will fall on the general budget.
findings.figures: £491k declining by £122k in 2025/26 to £368k
findings.quote: Included within current monitoring position funding subsidised routes and new contract with Arriva commencing August 2025

findings.headline: Afghan, Ukrainian, and asylum seeker resettlement schemes consume £3.6m of reserves with commitments extending through 2029/30.
findings.detail: The council holds significant reserves for three resettlement schemes: Afghan Relocation (£2.7m), Ukrainian Refugee (£698k), and Asylum Seekers (£243k). These reserves are committed as part of the resettlement model and are being systematically drawn down through the forecast period. The Afghan reserve declines to £234k by 2029/30, Ukrainian to £66k, and asylum seekers to zero.
findings.matters: Statutory duties around asylum and refugee support are consuming substantial reserves; if grant funding is withdrawn or caseloads increase, the council would face immediate budget pressure.
findings.figures: Afghan Relocation £2.7m (declining to £234k); Ukrainian Refugee £698k (declining to £66k); Asylum Seekers £243k (declining to £0)
findings.quote: Committed as part of resettlement model

findings.headline: Job evaluation costs create a £7.61m reserve commitment with multi-year implications.
findings.detail: The budget strategy identifies job evaluation as a significant corporate commitment of £7.61m. The document notes this separately in the opening summary as a committed earmarked reserve item, suggesting this is a known cost that will need to be funded from reserves over the period.
findings.matters: Job evaluation is a substantial one-off cost that will consume reserves; if delayed or disputed, it could create additional pressure on the budget position.
findings.quote: Job Evaluation Provision for Job Evaluation work 7.61-

findings.headline: Total reserves declining by £33m over five years, from £79.3m to £46.3m.
findings.detail: The council's overall reserve position is contracting significantly. The document shows total reserves and balances declining from £79.3m at April 2025 to £46.3m by April 2030. This reflects planned drawdowns of earmarked reserves to support the Medium Term Financial Strategy.
findings.matters: Large reserve depletion indicates the council is consuming accumulated funds to manage its budget position; this reduces financial flexibility and contingency capacity for unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: Total reserves: £79.3m (April 2025) declining to £46.3m (April 2030)
findings.quote: Total Reserves and Balances 46.26

findings.headline: Financing costs rising from 7.1% to 8.1% of revenue stream as investment-backed borrowing grows to £260.8m
findings.detail: Council's debt service burden is increasing year-on-year. Financing costs (interest) as a proportion of net revenue stream projected to rise from 7.1% in 2025/26 to 8.1% by 2027/28. Total investments funded by borrowing growing from £185.9m to £260.8m over the same period, indicating accelerating debt-funded investment strategy.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs reduce financial flexibility; increasing portion of revenue committed to interest payments; sensitivity to further interest rate rises increases
findings.figures: Total investments funded by borrowing £260.821m by 31.3.27 (up from £185.871m at 31.3.25); financing costs 7.1% (2025/26) rising to 8.1% (2027/28)
findings.quote: Financing Costs (Interest) to Net Revenue Stream: 7.1% (2025/26 Forecast) 7.6% (2026/27 Forecast) 8.1% (2027/28 Forecast)

findings.headline: Investment income dependency rising to 6.6% of net service expenditure, with contingency plan relying on service reductions or balance-sheet depletion if returns underperform
findings.detail: Investment returns (interest, rental income, trading profits) are increasingly material to the revenue budget, growing from 5.6% of net service expenditure in 2024/25 to 6.6% forecast for 2026/27. Strategy explicitly acknowledges that if investments fail to achieve expected returns, contingency plans include service reductions, further savings, or drawing down reserves in the short term.
findings.matters: Growing dependency on investment performance creates revenue vulnerability; underperformance would force service cuts or rapid depletion of financial reserves
findings.figures: Investment income as proportion of net service expenditure: 5.6% (2024/25 actual) rising to 6.6% (2026/27 forecast)
findings.quote: Should it fail to achieve the expected net profit, the Authority's contingency plans for continuing to provide these services are that the revenue budget includes a contingency; the delivery of further savings; the use of balances (in the short-term)

findings.headline: Property portfolio valuation subject to revaluation during 2025/26 accounts; position to be reviewed if valuations fall below purchase cost
findings.detail: Council holds £254.4m in property investments through the Property Investment Portfolio and solar farm. Council treats investments as secure if valuations equal or exceed purchase cost. Document explicitly flags that if valuations fall below purchase cost during 2025/26 accounts process, the position will be formally reviewed, suggesting valuations could be at risk.
findings.matters: Property represents 64% of total investment exposure; revaluation shortfalls would weaken balance sheet and could constrain borrowing capacity; indicates uncertainty about asset values
findings.figures: Total property held for service and investment purposes £262.385m forecast for 31.3.27 (PIP £254.385m, solar farm £8m)
findings.quote: Should the 2025/26 financial year end accounts preparation and audit process value these properties below their purchase cost, then the position will be reviewed.

findings.headline: Loans to Nuplace Ltd growing to £95.7m, approaching the council's approved lending limit of £117m for this single entity
findings.detail: Council's wholly-owned housing company Nuplace is receiving increasing loans, forecast at £95.7m by March 2027, up from £62.3m in March 2025. Combined with share investment of £41m, total Nuplace exposure funded by borrowing will reach £136.7m. The approved lending limit of £117m means the council is nearing its self-imposed cap on direct lending to this entity.
findings.matters: Growing concentration of council borrowing in a single entity; approaching lending limits may constrain future flexibility and increases exposure if Nuplace performance deteriorates
findings.figures: Nuplace loans estimated £95.702m by 31.3.27 (up from £62.257m at 31.3.25); approved lending limit £117m; combined Nuplace debt and equity funded by borrowing £136.749m
findings.quote: Nuplace – wholly owned company Estimated Balance Due 31.3.27 95.702 Approved Limit £117m

findings.headline: £191.5m Property Investment Portfolio exposed to void and market risk; revenue liability from new builds capped at £350k annually
findings.detail: Council holds £191.5m property portfolio generating £10.3m rental income. Document identifies explicit risks including voids, bad debt, competitive market, and Telford's structural reliance on manufacturing sector. Cap on annual revenue liability from new proactive unit development set at £350k, suggesting prior void experience.
findings.matters: Large commercial property exposure creates downside risk if manufacturing-dependent Telford economy weakens or property market downturn occurs; void risk cap indicates council has managed or anticipates void periods.
findings.figures: £191.5m portfolio valuation, £10.3m annual rental income, £350k annual revenue liability cap on new proactive builds
findings.quote: At a macro level risk exists linked with changes in the commercial market and Telford's heavy reliance on the manufacturing sector.

findings.headline: Financing costs (interest and MRP) rising to 8.14% of net revenue stream by 2027/28, constraining discretionary funding
findings.detail: Interest and debt repayment charges increase from 7.09% of net revenue in 2025/26 to 8.14% in 2027/28 before declining. At 8%+ of the revenue budget, financing represents a substantial ongoing commitment against core service funding.
findings.matters: Financing charges of 8%+ of budget significantly constrain funds available for discretionary spending and indicate limited headroom for additional borrowing without service cuts.
findings.quote: Financing Cost as a proportion of net revenue stream 7.09% 2025/26, 7.64% 2026/27, 8.14% 2027/28, 7.96% 2028/29, 7.06% 2029/30

findings.headline: Council assumes 4.5% interest on £230m prudential borrowing; 1% rate increase would cost £2.3m annually
findings.detail: Planned prudential borrowing 2025/26-2029/30 totals £230m with assumed rates of 4.5% for 2026/27, declining to 3.5% from 2029/30. Council's rate assumptions trail recent market peaks, creating material exposure if rates persist above forecast.
findings.matters: Interest rate assumptions significantly lower than recent historical peaks; if rates remain elevated, council faces unbudgeted revenue pressure and reduced debt service affordability.
findings.figures: £230m prudential borrowing planned, 4.5% assumed for 2026/27, 1% rate increase = £2.3m annual exposure
findings.quote: Prudential borrowing 2025/26 to 2029/30 totals £230m (excluding refinancing existing loans maturing); 1% interest on this would in total be £2.3m.

findings.headline: Business Rates system redesign from 2026/27 creates material revenue uncertainty with potential for increased appeals
findings.detail: Significant changes beginning 2026/27 include introduction of three new multipliers, system reset, and property revaluation. Council explicitly flags this as creating uncertainty and heightened risk of appeals, with no mitigation strategy detailed yet.
findings.matters: Business rates is a major council revenue source; system reset and revaluation could reduce retained income or create unexpected appeals liability affecting cash flow and budget planning.
findings.figures: 3 new multipliers, system reset, and revaluation beginning 2026/27; quantified impact not yet known
findings.quote: The impact of the significant changes to the Business Rates Retention system from 2026/27 including the introduction of 3 new multipliers, a system reset and revaluation which could result in an increase in level of appeals

findings.headline: Borrowing increased by £64m in FY2024/25 to £434.9m, accelerating debt growth trajectory
findings.detail: Council's total borrowing increased 17% year-on-year to £434.9m, driven by capital programme financing. Capital Financing Requirement projected to reach £746.7m by 2028/29, continuing to rise significantly over the forecast period.
findings.matters: Significant year-on-year debt acceleration signals growing borrowing needs and limits future headroom; lenders monitor debt trajectory and cumulative exposure closely.
findings.figures: £434.9m total borrowing at March 2025, £64m increase from prior year, CFR £746.733m by 2028/29
findings.quote: Total borrowing at 31 March 2025 was £434.9m which was an increase of £64m compared to 31 March 2024 which related to the funding the approved capital programme.

findings.headline: Council explicitly states it will not allow budget pressure to force statutory service failures in Adult Social Care or Children's Safeguarding, raising risk of unplanned reserve depletion if demand exceeds investment.
findings.detail: The council commits: 'The Council is committed to ensuring that we always meet the assessed needs of vulnerable people as we make changes to services, we will always place priority on these essential services and will not let financial pressures mean that we fail to meet the assessed statutory needs of vulnerable residents.' This is a statutory obligation under the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014, but it means the council will use reserves before cutting these services. With Adult Social Care already described as 'under pressure,' in-year demand spikes could force unplanned reserve drawdown.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's spending priorities under stress. This statement tells a lender that Adult Social Care and Children's Safeguarding are protected at the expense of other services and reserves. It also signals that reserves will be drawn down to meet statutory duties if necessary—reducing the buffer the council has against unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: General and Special Fund balances: £4.4m at start of 2025/26; Budget Strategy Reserve: £21.7m available
findings.quote: The Council is committed to ensuring that we always meet the assessed needs of vulnerable people as we make changes to services, we will always place priority on these essential services and will not let financial pressures mean that we fail to meet the assessed statutory needs of vulnerable residents.

findings.headline: Business rates reset and revaluation from April 2026 introduces system-wide volatility and council explicitly flags risk of increased appeals.
findings.detail: The Government is implementing a business rates reset, revaluation (to reflect property values since 2023), and new multiplier system from April 2026. The council notes this will 'could result in an increase in level of appeals.' The settlement includes three new multipliers for Retail, Hospitality and Leisure (RHL) at 5p lower than existing, but also a new High-Value Multiplier for properties over £2m. The council does not quantify the net impact on its business rates income, only flags the appeals risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs certainty on tax income. The reset and revaluation are significant unknowns—a revaluation can move the dial significantly for a council. Increased appeals could delay revenue collection and create volatility in the year when the council is already facing a large structural gap. The council's projections assume business rates income will grow modestly, but the reset could shift that in either direction.
findings.figures: Business rates reset and revaluation effective 1 April 2026; three new multipliers; 3-year transitional relief scheme for businesses; projected business rates income (inc. s.31 grants) £60.809m in 2026/27
findings.quote: The changes to the Business Rates System effective from 1st April 2026 which introduce 3 new multipliers as well as a reset of the system and a revaluation... which could result in an increase in level of appeals.

findings.headline: By 2029/30, the council will have committed £169.1m to Nuplace and Telford & Wrekin Homes, making this a material balance sheet risk if returns deteriorate.
findings.detail: The council plans to invest a cumulative total of £169.1m in Nuplace and Telford & Wrekin Homes by the end of the MTFS period (2029/30). While the portfolio has appreciated 32% and generated £4.6m cumulative profit, the council is continuously expanding it. The MTFS projects 177 additional homes underway and ongoing investment through 2029/30. If the property market softens or rental income falls, the council's ability to close future budget gaps via these returns is at risk.
findings.matters: A lender evaluates covenant strength by looking at asset quality and realisability. A £169m portfolio of rental properties, while currently performing, is illiquid and market-sensitive. If the council faces a budget crisis in 2028–2029, it cannot quickly liquidate this without distress. The council is also assuming ongoing capital receipts from asset sales (£17.788m planned) to fund transformation—if property sales stall, the budget model breaks.
findings.figures: Total investment in Nuplace and Telford & Wrekin Homes by end 2029/30: £169.1m; current portfolio value £122.8m; Works underway to complete 177 additional homes; capital receipts planned £17.788m over medium term
findings.quote: By the end of the MTFS period, 2029/30, the Council's total investment in Nuplace and Telford & Wrekin Homes will be £169.1m since Nuplace was established, 1 April 2015

findings.headline: Council is dependent on £12.3m+ of commercial returns (Nuplace rental income £2m + Growth Fund £10.3m+) to balance the 2026/27 budget without using reserves.
findings.detail: The council states that if the proposed council tax increase and all £19.1m of savings are delivered, 'there is no requirement for the use of balances at present in 2026/27.' However, this assumes Nuplace generates £2m income and the Property Investment Portfolio delivers net additional income 'expected to exceed £10.3m.' These are commercial returns on £122.8m+ of council capital investment. Any shortfall would force either immediate balance drawdown or additional service cuts.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess asset quality and rental/income sustainability. Nuplace shows strong metrics (0.84% cumulative void rate, £4.6m cumulative profit), but the council is heavily leveraged to these returns. A void spike, rental decline, or economic downturn could force emergency reserve use or additional borrowing.
findings.figures: Nuplace income forecast £2m in 2025/26; Property Investment Portfolio net additional income expected to exceed £10.3m; Nuplace portfolio valued at £122.8m (as at 31 March 2025) with cumulative growth of 32%; cumulative profit before tax £4.6m since 2015/16
findings.quote: For 2025/26 income streams from Nuplace are projected at £2m after covering all additional costs and the net additional income from the Property Investment Portfolio boosted by benefits from the Telford Growth Fund is projected to exceed £10.3m.

findings.headline: Projected budget gaps of £9.2m (2027/28), £12.5m (2028/29), and £22.2m (2029/30) will require further savings or tax increases, with no clear plan.
findings.detail: The MTFS table shows that after the 4.99% council tax increase in 2026/27, the remaining budget gaps escalate: £9.243m in 2027/28, £12.494m in 2028/29, and £22.211m in 2029/30. These gaps are explicitly described as 'to find from further savings/use of balances/council tax increases in future years.' The council offers no pathway for closing them. The report notes that 'projections of what the council's budget gap might be in 2027/28, and later years are therefore extremely difficult to make.'
findings.matters: A lender needs assurance about the council's medium-term financial trajectory. Gaps of £22m by year 4, with no plan and acknowledged uncertainty, suggest the council may face a sudden funding crisis or emergency support request (EFS). 29 councils required EFS in 2025/26; Telford's gap projection puts it at risk.
findings.figures: Budget gap 2027/28: £9.243m; 2028/29: £12.494m; 2029/30: £22.211m (before any council tax increase beyond 2026/27)
findings.quote: To find from further savings/use of balances/council tax increases in future years: 0 [2026/27], 9,243 [2027/28], 12,494 [2028/29], 22,211 [2029/30]

findings.headline: Adult social care services remain under severe pressure despite £15.8m additional investment and are the driver of the entire budget strategy.
findings.detail: The council is investing £15.8m net additional funding into Adult Social Care in 2026/27 and £2.7m into Children's Safeguarding. Yet the MTFS explicitly states that 'Adult Social Care services are facing pressure despite the significant additional ongoing investments made in recent years, additional ongoing investment is therefore required.' The council budget allocates nearly £150m combined to these two areas—70% of the net revenue budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's assessment of 'adequate investment' in social care is realistic. If demand continues to outpace the £15.8m injection, the council will face uncontrollable in-year pressures or service failures. The fact that the council is still describing this as 'pressure' after investment signals the problem is structural, not cyclical.
findings.figures: £15.8m additional net investment in Adult Social Care; £2.7m in Children's Safeguarding; nearly £150m combined commitment (70% of net revenue base budget); population aged 65+ increased 27.6% in decade to 2024 vs England average 15.5%
findings.quote: Adult Social Care has faced significant additional pressures from the increase in the number of people needing access to social care services and specialist care. The Borough's population increased by 14.9% in the decade to 2024... The population in the Borough for those aged 65 plus increased by 27.6% in the decade to 2024, in comparison to England's 15.5% increase.

findings.headline: Cumulative savings burden now projected at £235.4m by 2029/30, with only four consecutive budgets available before exhausting practical options.
findings.detail: The council has already delivered £195.3m of ongoing budget savings since 2009/10. This MTFS proposes a further £19.1m in 2026/27 and projects total savings of £235.7m by 2029/30. Each additional tranche becomes harder; the council notes that 'after already having delivered £195.3m of savings, these savings now put forward will include some proposals that are more challenging.'
findings.matters: A council that has already cut nearly a quarter of a billion pounds faces diminishing returns and rising political/service-delivery risk on each new tranche. A lender needs assurance that further cuts are credible and won't force service failures or emergency borrowing.
findings.figures: £195.3m savings delivered to end 2025/26; £19.1m new savings proposed for 2026/27 onwards; £235.7m total projected by end 2029/30
findings.quote: By the end of the current financial year, the Council will have delivered ongoing budget savings, including additional income, of £195.3m since 2009/10. Despite the proposed £1.20 per week (Band B) council tax increase (which includes the ASC precept) which will raise around £4.7m, it is necessary for the Council to find further budget savings in order to deliver a balanced budget without using an unsustainable level of one-off balances.

findings.paper_title: Housing Investment Programme - Update Business Plan Cabinet FINAL v1
findings.headline: Renters' Rights Act 2025 and Building Safety Act 2022 will reshape landlord obligations and create new compliance costs
findings.detail: Major legislative reforms are underway, including energy efficiency mandates and compliance reforms. While the document states Nuplace is 'well set to respond', the scale and cost of compliance with new tenant rights, energy standards, and building safety regimes is not quantified. This creates operational cost uncertainty.
findings.matters: New regulatory compliance costs may reduce operating margins and require capital investment in retrofit/compliance; a lender needs to know whether these have been costed and funded
findings.figures: No cost figures provided
findings.quote: The Renters' Rights Act 2025, combined with energy efficiency mandates and compliance reforms (The Building Safety Act 2022 and Energy Efficiency & Sustainability Legislation), aims to improve tenant security, housing quality, and transparency. These changes will reshape landlord obligations, tenancy structures, and enforcement mechanisms over the next decade.

findings.paper_title: Housing Investment Programme - Update Business Plan Cabinet FINAL v1
findings.headline: 145 of 303 pipeline homes require additional budget approvals not yet secured
findings.detail: Of the proposed expansion, 158 homes are deliverable within existing approvals (£34.8m capital), but 145 additional homes require further budget decisions. This means funding for over a third of the pipeline is not yet committed, and the council will need to approve additional expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender assessing the council's capital headroom and borrowing needs must know that this expansion is only partially committed; further borrowing or capital allocation may be required
findings.figures: 158 homes approved (£34.8m); 145 homes pending approval
findings.quote: Circa 158 of these homes are deliverable within existing budget approvals, representing a capital investment of £34.8m. Delivery of a further possible 145 homes will require additional budget approvals.

findings.paper_title: Housing Investment Programme - Update Business Plan Cabinet FINAL v1
findings.headline: Higher interest rates have increased borrowing costs for Nuplace, reducing project viability
findings.detail: Development debt has become more expensive, squeezing the financial case for schemes. The document expects this to improve if base rates continue to fall in 2026, but it has already impacted viability assessments on the current pipeline.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know that the council's housing company is exposed to rate rises and that scheme returns are sensitive to financing costs
findings.figures: No specific cost quantum given
findings.quote: higher interest rates having increased borrowing costs for Nuplace, making development debt more expensive and reducing project viability

findings.paper_title: Housing Investment Programme - Update Business Plan Cabinet FINAL v1
findings.headline: Construction costs have risen 15–20% since 2020 with further 2.7% increase expected in 2026, compounding scheme viability challenges
findings.detail: The council faces sustained inflation in build costs. This directly reduces the viability buffer on pipeline schemes. The document notes BTR starts nationally fell 50% in 2023 compared to 2022, partly due to cost pressures. Falling base rates expected to help, but construction cost inflation remains a headwind.
findings.matters: Rising construction costs reduce the return on capital invested and may force scheme cuts or higher borrowing, affecting the program's financial case
findings.figures: 15–20% rise since 2020; 2.7% further increase expected 2026
findings.quote: construction costs, which have increased by 15-20% since 2020 and are expected to continue to rise by circa 2.7% in 2026

findings.headline: Government Local Government Finance Settlement reforms create planning uncertainty at the same time as sector-wide pressures
findings.detail: The council notes the Government is undertaking the most significant local government finance reform in over two decades, with 2026/27 planned as the first year of a new funding regime. While there will be transitional measures, detailed implications for Telford & Wrekin will not be known until the provisional settlement is announced just before Christmas. This uncertainty comes against a background of the council having delivered £181.7m in ongoing budget savings since 2009/10.
findings.matters: Planning uncertainty at the sector level compounds the council's ability to forecast medium-term finances reliably, particularly given it has already achieved substantial cumulative savings
findings.figures: £181.7m ongoing budget savings since 2009/10
findings.quote: The reform of funding arrangements is the most significant change in over two decades. There are likely to be winners and losers and transitional mechanisms will be crucial to avoid services being put at risk. This context makes financial planning extremely challenging. The funding outlook for the medium term therefore remains very uncertain and will clearly continue to be challenging, particularly given the Council has already had to deliver £181.7m ongoing budget savings since 2009/10.

findings.headline: DSG deficit expected to grow by up to £5m during 2025/26, building on existing £4.66m deficit
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit carried forward from 2024/25 was £4.66m, made up of £1.82m from 2023/24 plus £2.84m in-year overspend. This deficit is expected to increase further by up to £5m during 2025/26 due to high needs budget pressures. This is a national issue but reflects continuing growth in demand for high needs educational support.
findings.matters: While DSG deficits are ring-fenced separately, they indicate structural pressures in education spending that affect overall council sustainability and financial planning
findings.figures: £4.66m deficit carried forward from 2024/25; expected increase of up to £5m during 2025/26; national DSG deficit was £2.148bn at end of 2023/24 and expected to increase substantially
findings.quote: It is anticipated that the deficit will increase further, by up to £5m during 2025/26. There continues to be pressure throughout the high needs system, due to increasing numbers of children and young people needing additional educational support.

findings.headline: All contingencies exhausted to achieve break-even, with no in-year buffer for unforeseen pressures
findings.detail: Before application of contingencies, the council was projected £7.2m over budget. The council is using all £3.95m general contingency, £1.25m of one-off contingency for general pressures, and £2.0m of one-off contingency for social care pressures to achieve a zero variance projection. This leaves no headroom for further pressures during the remainder of the year.
findings.matters: Using all contingencies to achieve break-even indicates the council has limited financial flexibility and resilience to handle unexpected costs or income shortfalls mid-year
findings.figures: £7.2m projected pressures before contingencies; £3.95m general contingency used; £3.25m specific contingencies used; £4.1m General Balance and £21.7m Budget Strategy Reserve remain unused but available
findings.quote: The current projected position would require use of all contingencies.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care pressures of £13.92m driven by unprecedented increase in people needing long-term residential care
findings.detail: The council is experiencing sustained and significant increase in people needing long-term residential care, largely older people. This is primarily driven by Telford & Wrekin's ageing population - the percentage of people aged 65+ increased by 35.7% compared to 20.1% across England. The council is mitigating this with £4.94m in savings and cost avoidance through a home first approach.
findings.matters: This is a structural demographic pressure that affects the council's ability to sustain services and manage its budget in future years, directly impacting financial stability for lenders assessing the council's creditworthiness
findings.figures: £13.92m additional investment needed; £4.94m in savings and cost avoidance; 35.7% increase in 65+ population vs 20.1% England average
findings.quote: During the year, there has been a sustained and significant increase in the number of new people who need long-term residential care, largely older people, although the rate of growth has slowed in September and October. Over the last census period, the percentage of people aged 65+ in Telford & Wrekin increased by 35.7% compared to 20.1% across England.

news_drafts.headline: Council approved £17m of new prudential borrowing across 2026/27–2028/29 to fund regeneration and leisure schemes.
news_drafts.lead: New borrowing commitments increase the council's debt burden and future interest costs at a time when the council is already under demand pressure in core services. The council needs to demonstrate it can service this debt and maintain its financial…

news_drafts.headline: Council Tax collection fell 0.41% below target to 96.89%, driven by Universal Credit transitions reducing support.
news_drafts.lead: This is a structural change in the council's tax base that will not reverse. As more claimants transition to Universal Credit, the council should expect lower collection rates as a permanent feature, reducing the income available for services.

news_drafts.headline: Sales Ledger debt collection shortfall of 3.34%, driven by a large unpaid balance from the Integrated Care Board.
news_drafts.lead: Income collection shortfalls reduce resources available for services. A large single debtor (the ICB) represents concentration risk — if that debt proves uncollectable, it creates a sudden pressure. Social Care debt from the health system is particularly…
